plain_english: But suppose your life has become full of trouble. You didn't see it coming, but you've fallen into a trap that either public or private fortune set for you. You can't untie it or break free. Remember this: prisoners suffer terribly at first from the chains around their legs. But once they stop fighting the chains and accept them, necessity teaches them to bear the weight with courage. Habit makes it easier. In every situation in life, you'll find ways to enjoy yourself, to relax, to find pleasure — as long as you're willing to make light of your troubles instead of hating them.
original_excerpt: Suppose, however, that your life has become full of trouble, and that without knowing what you were doing you have fallen into some snare which either public or private Fortune has set for you, and that you can neither untie it nor break it: then remember that fettered men suffer much at first from the burdens and clogs upon their legs: afterwards, when they have made up their minds not to fret themselves about them, but to endure them, necessity teaches them to bear them bravely, and habit to bear them easily. In every station of life you will find amusements, relaxations, and enjoyments; that is, provided you be willing to make light of evils rather than to hate them.

plain_english: Since we know what sorrows we're born into, we should thank Nature for nothing more than giving us habit. Habit softens misfortune and helps us get used to even the worst troubles. No one could survive misfortune if it kept hitting us with the same force it has when it first strikes. We are all chained to Fortune. Some people's chains are loose and made of gold. Others have tight chains made of cheaper metal. But what difference does it make? We're all prisoners together. Even the people who chained us are chained themselves — unless you think a chain on your left side weighs less than one on your right. One person might be bound by public office, another by wealth. Some carry the burden of famous birth, others of humble birth. Some must obey other people's commands, others only their own. Some are stuck in one place because they were banished there, others because they were chosen for the priesthood. All life is slavery. So each person should accept their situation, complain as little as possible, and grab whatever good they can find.
original_excerpt: Knowing to what sorrows we were born, there is nothing for which Nature more deserves our thanks than for having invented habit as an alleviation of misfortune, which soon accustoms us to the severest evils. No one could hold out against misfortune if it permanently exercised the same force as at its first onset. We are all chained to Fortune: some men's chain is loose and made of gold, that of others is tight and of meaner metal: but what difference does this make? we are all included in the same captivity, and even those who have bound us are bound themselves, unless you think that a chain on the left side is lighter to bear: one man may be bound by public office, another by wealth: some have to bear the weight of illustrious, some of humble birth: some are subject to the commands of others, some only to their own: some are kept in one place by being banished thither, others by being elected to the priesthood. All life is slavery: let each man therefore reconcile himself to his lot, complain of it as little as possible, and lay hold of whatever good lies within his reach.

plain_english: No situation is so terrible that a fair mind can't find some good in it. Even tiny spaces can serve many purposes if you arrange them cleverly. Good planning can make even the smallest room livable. Use your common sense when facing problems. You can soften what feels harsh, expand what feels cramped, and make heavy loads feel lighter when you carry them with skill.
original_excerpt: No condition can be so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it. Small sites, if ingeniously divided, may be made use of for many different purposes, and arrangement will render ever so narrow a room habitable. Call good sense to your aid against difficulties: it is possible to soften what is harsh, to widen what is too narrow, and to make heavy burdens press less severely upon one who bears them skilfully.

plain_english: We shouldn't let our desires chase after distant things. Instead, we should focus them on what's nearby and achievable. Our desires won't tolerate being completely shut down. We must avoid things that either can't happen or would be extremely hard to get. Instead, we should pursue what's close at hand and within reach. Always remember that all things are equally unimportant. They may look different on the outside, but inside they're all equally empty.
original_excerpt: Moreover, we ought not to allow our desires to wander far afield, but we must make them confine themselves to our immediate neighbourhood, since they will not endure to be altogether locked up. We must leave alone things which either cannot come to pass or can only be effected with difficulty, and follow after such things as are near at hand and within reach of our hopes, always remembering that all things are equally unimportant, and that though they have a different outward appearance, they are all alike empty within.

plain_english: Don't envy those in high positions. What looks impressive from down here is actually steep and dangerous. When cruel fate puts people in risky situations, they'll be safer if they show less pride in their status. They should do everything they can to bring their fortunes down to everyone else's level. Many people have to cling to their high positions because they can't step down without falling hard. They tell us their worst burden is having to burden others. They say they're nailed to their high post rather than lifted up to it. So let them help themselves by freely giving out justice, mercy, and kindness. This will give them something to cushion their fall. Looking ahead to this possibility, they can hold their position with more hope.
original_excerpt: Neither let us envy those who are in high places: the heights which look lofty to us are steep and rugged. Again, those whom unkind fate has placed in critical situations will be safer if they show as little pride in their proud position as may be, and do all they are able to bring down their fortunes to the level of other men's. There are many who must needs cling to their high pinnacle of power, because they cannot descend from it save by falling headlong: yet they assure us that their greatest burden is being obliged to be burdensome to others, and that they are nailed to their lofty post rather than raised to it: let them then, by dispensing justice, clemency, and kindness with an open and liberal hand, provide themselves with assistance to break their fall, and looking forward to this maintain their position more hopefully.

plain_english: Nothing frees us from swinging between hope and fear like setting our own limits on success. Don't let Fortune decide when to stop your career — stop on your own terms, well before you think you need to. This way, you'll still have desires that motivate you. But they'll stay within bounds and won't drag you into huge, vague projects.
original_excerpt: Yet nothing sets us free from these alternations of hope and fear so well as always fixing some limit to our successes, and not allowing Fortune to choose when to stop our career, but to halt of our own accord long before we apparently need do so. By acting thus certain desires will rouse up our spirits, and yet being confined within bounds, will not lead us to embark on vast and vague enterprises.
